speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The justification for this change was to safeguard minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of Members of Parliament (MPs) from GRCs were limited to a range of 25% to 50%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, the GRC system has evolved for varying reasons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 1996, the size of a GRC was raised again, this time to a maximum of six candidates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This meant that the upper limit on MPs from GRCs was effectively increased to about 90%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, will elaborate further on the changes to the GRC system over the years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will now talk about the weaknesses of the GRC system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the objective of ensuring minority representation in Parliament is laudable, the GRC system brings along other consequences that are undesirable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A common complaint about the GRC system is that MPs are not necessarily elected on their own merits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The team approach allows some Members to ride on the coat-tails of other more established or popular team members.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Consider a GRC with two teams of four candidates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If all the candidates were to contest in four separate SMCs, voters could have selected two candidates from Team A and two candidates from Team B as the ones they feel most suitable to represent them in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as they can only vote for one team or the other, the result is the loss of two stronger candidates and the election of two weaker candidates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This illustration shows how the GRC system can lead to a sub-optimal outcome for voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Former Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said in 2006 that the GRC system helped the People’s Action Party (PAP) recruitment efforts by giving potential candidates the assurance of a good chance of winning.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I interpret this as open acknowledgment that the coat-tail effect was intentional and the GRC was intended to enhance the chances of the PAP winning at the expense of the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, indeed, it took more than 20 years before the strongest Opposition party was able to win a GRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such an approach, however, encourages the “kiasu”, or fear to lose, syndrome, breeds a generation of politicians sheltered from tough electoral battles and sets unsustainable expectations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All it took was one electoral loss for Singapore politics to lose some Ministers permanently.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PAP has said that if voters do not vote for the PAP's team, key Ministers will disappear from the Cabinet.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a portrayal attempts to hold voters to ransom.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also hampered the political development of Singapore by setting higher and higher hurdles for the Opposition parties which are much weaker compared to the ruling party.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In an SMC, candidates need the support of their constituents to win elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their election outcome is more directly controlled by voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a GRC, however, the election outcome is also dependent on which team a candidate is placed in, which is a decision made by party leaders.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It becomes unclear whether voters' decision or party leader's decision play a bigger part.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Voters' influence on election outcome is thus reduced under a GRC system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, many MPs in GRCs have vacated their seats for various reasons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some passed away, some resigned over conduct that compromised their ability to serve as MPs, and others resigned to stand in Presidential Elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In each of these cases, no by-election was held to fill these vacancies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because by-elections are expressly not required to be called when a vacancy arises in a GRC, unless the entire slate of MPs representing a GRC vacate their seats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government explained that this is to prevent any individual MP in a GRC from holding the other MPs in the same GRC to ransom.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this also has the effect of depriving residents in these GRCs of an elected representative in Parliament, which is highly undesirable, given our system of representative democracy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This issue has been debated several times before in this House.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 1999, following the resignation of Mr Choo Wee Khiang as an MP of Jalan Besar GRC, Mr JB Jeyaratnam moved a Motion for this House to resolve that a writ of election should be issued to fill the vacancy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During his speech, Mr Jeyaratnam noted that: "Jalan Besar GRC voters are entitled to four MPs in Parliament", and "that is their constitutional right".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's response to Mr Jeyaratnam's point at that time was most unsatisfactory.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then-Leader of the House, Mr Wong Kan Seng, claimed that there was no diminution of voters' constitutional rights because, "They voted for the four MPs and the MPs carry on" and "the voters, in fact, voted with the knowledge that should a vacancy arise, such a vacancy need not be filled as provided for in our law".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Wong's response does not address the underlying issue, which is that the voters of Jalan Besar GRC voted for a team of four MPs with four votes to represent them in this House.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When a vacancy arises in a GRC, the voters of that GRC have lost a vote in Parliament to represent their interest.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other MPs in the GRC cannot take over the voting rights or the Parliamentary Question quota or the right to raise an Adjournment Motion of the MP that has resigned.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the Parliamentary level, the rights of the GRC voters are unquestionably diminished when an unfilled vacancy arises in a GRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is particularly pertinent when the Member of Parliament who has resigned is the minority representative for that GRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The vacancy undermines the primary objective of the GRC system, which is to ensure minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the constituency level, while the remaining MPs in the team can help to cover for their former teammate in house visits and Meet-the-People sessions, something somewhere has to give.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As former Nominated Member of Parliament (NMP), Prof Thio Li-ann, pointed out in her Motion in 2008: "MPs have punishing schedules".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MPs have to juggle their responsibilities in their full-time jobs, their Parliamentary duties, their constituency duties, their party duties, and their personal and family lives.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If their constituency duties increased due to covering for a vacancy, there must be a corresponding cut somewhere else.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cut could be in the area of Parliamentary duties, the quality in carrying out constituency duties, or sacrificing their personal or family lives, none of which is fair nor desirable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the PAP intend to regularly repeat this?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Running in a GE is an inherent promise to serve the residents for a term of five years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Breaking that promise is not something that should be taken lightly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, therefore, troubling if such broken promises were to occur at regular intervals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a vacancy will not be filled via a by-election, residents are underserved and under-represented for the sake of the party's other motivations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did the party not plan for this expected vacancy when it went into GE 2020?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could it not have informed voters of this possibility or selected its candidate from an SMC so that residents are not underserved?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It can also be argued that a team without Senior Minister Tharman is not what the voters in Jurong GRC voted for.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister Tharman has served many terms as an MP and in various senior positions in Public Service, while the other team members are relatively new.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The case that a team without Senior Minister Tharman makes for a material difference is overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is analogous to having the terms of a contract changed materially and unilaterally midway through by one party but the other party remained bound to the contract until expiry.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any other context, this would not have been accepted.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not have GRCs, only SMCs, then these problems would not exist.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ensuring minority representation is the justification for the GRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the GRC is purportedly to protect minority interests, it paradoxically entrenches racial lines and promotes the belief that minority candidates are unable to win elections on their own merits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) is confident that Singaporeans do not vote along racial lines and minority candidates are well able to win elections on their own merits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though the majority of voters are Chinese, many non-Chinese candidates have won elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before the introduction of GRCs, in GE 1984, minority candidates have won in SMCs against majority candidates; for example, Mr JB Jeyaratnam, Mr Zulkifli Mohammed, Mr Abbas Abu Amin, and so on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More recently, we also have Mr Michael Palmer and Mr Murali Pillai.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In GRCs, we have the Aljunied team where three out of the five MPs are non-Chinese.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister Tharman is one of the most popular politicians and his decision to contest in the Presidential Election showed his confidence that Singaporeans do not vote along racial lines.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if the PAP is not convinced, there are other ways to ensure adequate minority representation in Parliament without the problems that come with the GRC system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would like to offer two alternatives here for consideration and debate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this scheme, minority candidates contest in SMCs just like other candidates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If enough minority candidates are elected, this scheme does not kick in.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, should there be under-representation of minorities, minority candidates who did not win the election but had the highest percentage of votes can be appointed as NCMPs to ensure adequate minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Residents from all constituencies can approach these NCMPs for assistance.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we are all familiar with the NCMP scheme for Opposition candidates, this scheme requires little explanation and minimal disruption to our current model.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another way of ensuring minority representation in Parliament is to adopt some form of proportional representation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under this system, a party that obtained 10% of the national votes will be allocated about 10% of the seats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When responding to a Motion brought forward by Prof Thio Li-ann in 2008, the Prime Minister said that our electoral system is designed to encourage voters to think very carefully not only about the individual that they want to represent them in Parliament but also the party that they want to form the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we want voters to vote for a political party instead of a candidate, the logical step is to move towards a system of party-list, proportional representation, where parties put forth a list of candidates for election.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Seats are then allocated to each political party based on their national vote share.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on the seats allocated, each party then selects the candidates on its party list to take up the seats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Proportional representation seeks to move the representation in Parliament closer to the national vote share to better reflect the wishes of the voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us first look at how this is done in other countries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there are countries fully on the proportional representation system like Israel and Sweden, there are also a number of countries with a hybrid system containing both first-past-the-post and proportional representation elements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The election in our constituencies is an example of the first-past-the-post system where the candidates with the highest votes get the seats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can adapt this system to ensure minority representation by stipulating a multiracial slate for SMC contests and a multiracial party list.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each party must select from the list to meet minimum racial representation requirements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have presented these shortcomings and offered two alternatives to ensure minority representation in Parliament for consideration and debate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intention here is not to call for immediate action but for thought and discussion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are still two years away from the next GE and have time to mull over this matter.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, the mixed proportional representation alternative is a major departure from our current system and requires more time and a fuller discussion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We call on the House and all Singaporeans to consider the alternatives that we have proposed to guarantee minority representation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that unlike the GRC system, these alternatives will strengthen our system of representative democracy and maximise democratic choice for voters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time for the GRC system to go.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge all Members to support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The introduction of the GRC system was part of a package of constitutional innovations during the 1980s which also included the introduction of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 1980s was a politically significant era for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It began with Mr JB Jeyaretnam breaking the Parliamentary dominance of the PAP during the 1981 Anson by-election.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Later, the 1984 General Election saw a 13% swing against the PAP and the election of two opposition Members – Mr JB Jeyaretnam and Mr Chiam See Tong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All these took place amidst a changing of guard in the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew and the other old guard Ministers retired.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 2G team led by Mr Goh Chok Tong took over.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PAP has always denied accusations that the introduction of the GRC system and the elected presidency was to entrench its political dominance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the beginning, both Constitutional innovations were meant to fulfil a specific purpose.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This became increasingly important as resettlement and the creation of Housing and Development Board (HDB) new towns under the Ethnic Integration Policy meant that there were no longer any more Malay majority constituencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think that many Singaporeans would have no objections with these schemes if these schemes stayed true to their original purpose.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, both the GRC system and the Elected Presidency have been subject to many changes over the years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although these changes had various justifications, it is still difficult for the public to be convinced that these frequent changes are not motivated by political considerations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, when the GRC system was introduced during the 1988 GE, all GRCs had three members.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was later expanded to a maximum of four in the 1991 GE.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason given by the then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong was to provide flexibility so that we could minimise major changes of boundaries to GRCs which have grown too big for the number of MPs serving them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But then in the 1991 General Election, the Opposition won an unprecedented four seats in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was followed by further tweaks to the GRC system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prime Minister Goh justified this move by claiming that he wanted to devolve more authority to the local communities by setting up Community Development Councils (CDCs).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because CDCs needed economies of scale and a critical mass of residents, Prime Minister Goh said that increasing the maximum number of MPs in the GRC from four to six will give more flexibility to the Electoral Boundaries Review Committee (EBRC) to configure a GRC which is the right size for this purpose.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans, including myself, have never been convinced by this reasoning.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Community Development Councils (CDCs) can be formed by forming six adjourning SMCs or two three-member GRCs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, many Singaporeans believed that the PAP Government expanded GRC sizes to hamper the Opposition's electoral chances after a strong showing by the Opposition in the 1991 GE.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are several ways in which GRCs can be used to maximise the PAP's advantages.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since 1988, SMCs that have been absorbed into GRCs have had a higher average vote share for the opposition than the average SMC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many of these SMCs, the Opposition polled above 40%, such as Braddell Heights, Bukit Batok and Changi in 1991, Joo Chiat in 2011 and Fengshan in 2015.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only SMCs and GRCs that the Opposition have won are consistently spared from changes in their electoral boundaries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I therefore fully expect West Coast GRC and other constituencies where the PSP contested in the last election to disappear or have their boundaries heavily redrawn in the next election.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that happens, I hope Singaporeans will open their eyes and decide for themselves if these changes are for population shifts and housing developments, or for other reasons.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result of the GRC boundaries, many HDB towns and planning areas in Singapore are fragmented among multiple GRCs and by extension, Town Councils and CDCs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, Serangoon Town is divided between Marine Parade GRC which is in Southeast CDC, Aljunied GRC which is in Northeast CDC and Ang Mo Kio GRC which is in Central Singapore CDC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The EBRC has never explained the reason for drawing such peculiar boundaries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such an arrangement can hardly foster a sense of community among local communities, which the PAP Government has claimed is the purpose of the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It instead gives rise to suspicion amongst Singaporeans that the PAP is manipulating the GRC system for their political benefit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is unlike SMCs, where a smaller number of voters creates more opportunities for divergence in election results.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given our first-past-the-post voting system, where the winning party wins all the seats in the GRC, the GRC system magnifies the electoral advantages of the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is why there is a very high level of disproportionality in the translation of Opposition votes to Parliament seats in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is due in a large part to the advantages that the GRC system provides for the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the 2006 GE, there has been some positive changes to the GRC system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prime Minister Lee has pledged to reduce the average size of GRCs and increase the number of SMCs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now there are also no more six-Member GRCs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the maximum size of GRCs in the Constitution is still six.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, these jumbo GRCs could still make a comeback in future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is by the grace of the Prime Minister, rather than by law, that we now have smaller GRCs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong can share during today's debate whether he will make the same commitment to having smaller GRCs once he takes over as the next Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister exercises great power over electoral boundaries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He gets to decide when the EBRC is formed; who is in the EBRC; and sets the terms of reference for the EBRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will Deputy Prime Minister Wong share his future approach towards electoral boundaries?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have just recounted how the PAP has frequently changed the rules around GRCs over the years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a similar story with the Elected Presidency which has been the subject of numerous Constitutional amendments over the years, most notably in 2016.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Presidential Election in 2011, Dr Tan Cheng Bock lost to Dr Tony Tan by a razor-thin margin of 0.35%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of those who voted for Dr Tan Cheng Bock hoped that he would be able to stand again during the Presidential Election in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In January 2016, Prime Minister Lee announced that it was timely to review the eligibility criteria of the Elected Presidency and convened a constitutional commission to do so.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At that point in time, he stated that any legislation to give effect to the Commission's recommendation would be tabled before the end of 2016, but this did not explicitly mean that any changes would be effective from the 2017 Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Commission eventually recommended that provision should be made for a Reserved Election if a particular race has not been elected for five Presidential terms.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was because the Elected Presidency had to be an integral pillar of Singapore's commitment to multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Constitutional Commission also did not make any recommendation regarding when the changes should be implemented.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was the Government that made the decision to start counting from President Wee Kim Wee, which meant that the 2017 Election would be a Reserved Election for Malay candidates only.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was also implemented at the 2017 Election.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All this came after Dr Tan Cheng Bock announced his intention to contest the 2017 Presidential Election on 11 March 2016, months before the Constitutional Commission released its report.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This same criterion was also used to disqualify the two Malay candidates who had wanted to stand in the first reserved Election for the Presidency in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would not be remiss to say that all this cast a dark shadow over the historic Presidency of President Halimah Yacob, who is our first female President and the first Malay President in 46 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It magnifies the seat share of the PAP beyond its voting strength and creates opportunities for the manipulation of electoral boundaries for partisan purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over time, it breeds cynicism and disillusion in our political system as the views of the public are not properly reflected in the election results.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the last 40 years, the PAP has won more than two-thirds of the votes only in the 2001 and 2015 GEs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our system, any political party commanding more than 50% will be able to form a stable government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One with more than 67% of the seats, or two-thirds majority will be able to amend the Constitution at will and thus, will be able to form a very strong government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The overwhelming PAP's supermajority of 90% is thus not necessary for a strong government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The supermajority only makes it more difficult for the Opposition to voice out the people's concerns adequately in the Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP supports the abolition of the GRC system to create a fairer and more representative Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A call to abolish the GRC system by an Opposition party is not new one.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In a 2014 paper, the National Solidarity Party (NSP) called for this as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It was also in the Workers' Party's (WP) 2020 elections manifesto under the heading "Accountable Political and Governance Institutions".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The NSP's key argument against the GRC system was that it essentially gave more power to a voted-in GRC because theoretically, one vote could elect several MPs, while in an SMC, one vote goes to elect only one MP.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: NSP's Secretary-General called this a lack of parity between the weight of the votes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The paper further added that in Singapore at that time, winning an election by appealing to the voters on the basis of ethnicity was highly improbable.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It said that it was highly improbable, which means that the NSP acknowledged that going down this line was a gamble.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It felt that the odds were good, but it was nonetheless a gamble.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And it is perhaps in this regard that the people also called for the introduction of a "constituencies reserved for minority" scheme in which some SMCs would be reserved for minority candidates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The WP's argument in its manifesto was that Singapore had matured to a point that there is no evidence now that Singaporeans vote solely along racial lines.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The PSP has made further arguments today about why the GRC advantages the ruling party and disadvantages others and may not be in the interest of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I must add that a Parliament where all Members are Chinese would have been a conceivable outcome of elections.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Given that even as we call ourselves a multiracial society, our population is in fact overwhelmingly Chinese and, as such, it falls to reason that there is likely to be more Chinese candidates from both the ruling party and the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Some opposition parties have previously expressed that it was difficult for them to attract enough good minority candidates to field several GRCs at that time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, it would also have been possible that in the absence of GRCs, the slate of smaller opposition parties may have been entirely, or overwhelmingly, Chinese.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The move to introduce GRCs in 1988 was not the first time that concern over minority representation had been raised and mitigating factors considered.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Government in the early 1980s had considered a twinning model where candidates would have to contest in a pair in some constituencies, with one being a minority.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This was dropped upon objection from minority MPs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And even at the start of Singapore's Independence, minority representation was a concern.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The 1966 Constitutional Commission chaired by the then Chief Justice considered this very question.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, this question of minority representation is one we have been pondering from the start of our Independence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The PSP Motion raises many questions that have been asked before and that have been answered before.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But PSP's position is that it is now the right time to reopen the matter and to relitigate on these questions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It appears to be also the position of other Opposition parties.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is therefore a currency to that proposal and I will come to this point on currency shortly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I have some questions as regards the Motion and the proposals made by PSP.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I will also venture to answer my own questions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is of course open to the PSP and indeed, any other party to disagree or agree with my answers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My first question is: does the PSP accept that there is no perfect electoral system?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we were to abolish the GRC system, then we would revert to an SMC first-past-the-post system – it is called the majority-to-reality system, within a Westminster Parliamentary Model.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: SMCs have been criticised on various grounds, and alternatives like a party-list system had been proposed, which is a form of proportional representation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards to the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, there are also a large number of criticisms.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such systems have been criticised for excluding minority parties who have won a particular share of the vote but did not manage to get past the post in any or many single-seat constituencies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It can lead to scenarios where a party can win over 40% of the vote but has little or no representation in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The FPTP system has also been found to be very difficult for minority and women candidates to do well in.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They have encouraged the development of ethnic-based parties given rise to regional fiefdoms and resulted in large numbers of wasted votes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are many criticisms of the FPTP system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have mentioned only some of the criticisms that have been raised by analysts and academics.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And in fact, the Westminster system itself has been criticised on various grounds, but I would not go into details on this.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, for other types of systems, proportional representation, for example, is criticised for giving rise to gridlock in decision-making due to fractured legislatures.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And the other systems, Sir, block vote systems, transferrable vote systems.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are so many of them and all of them have advantages and disadvantages.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, the PSP proposal is not a proposal to move to a perfect electoral system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is a move to revert to a prior electoral system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And it is not even a proposal to correct the system but a proposal to transit to what is, in fact, another imperfect system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even if we were to abolish the GRC system, Sir, and move and revert to what we had before, there would be criticisms of it – there would be advantages and there would be disadvantages as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The question really is whether what the PSP is proposing is the best system in Singapore's context.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, the PSP has proposed an NCMP for minorities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The question that arises here is whether we will be able to accept; will Singaporeans be able to accept a scenario in which many or most of our minority MPs are NCMPs?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They would have no constituency experience and is it acceptable for most Singaporeans who have exposure only to a Chinese elected MP?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, as regards to proportional representation, I mentioned earlier some of the disadvantages, but all the countries that the hon Member Ms Poa referred to, are countries that have proportional representation systems that are not based on ethnicity, but they are instead based on party.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One of the things that we need to think about is how this proposed system would square with the Westminster parliamentary system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, how would the MPs elected be allocated to their constituencies?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And, indeed, one of the criticisms of a proportional representation system is that it fails to provide a strong geographical linkage between an MP and an MP's electorate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And furthermore, a party-list system will subject all MPs, not only minority MPs, to the system, but it will provide a proviso for minorities, and this may lead to fractious legislatures.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Race may not now be a consideration in the elections, not despite the GRC system but because of it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And the GRC system simply takes questions of race, religion and all of these other potentially divisive qualities out of the equation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further to this, race is largely removed as a strategic consideration in how parties decide which candidate runs in which constituency.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we were to abolish the GRC system, I imagine that race would invariably become one of the important considerations in where candidates run or where they are placed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not believe that parties would just be deploying candidates around willy-nilly and simply hope for the best.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such a party would not likely do well in the elections.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But what would happen if we abolished GRCs would be that race and religion would creep back into the party's considerations when determining their elections strategy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the GRC system has also worked to ensure that all parties contesting in the elections and in GRCs must themselves be multiracial.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And tellingly and surprisingly, I found that both of the PSP hon Members did not address whether the GRC system had achieved its original purpose in the first place of ensuring minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, does the PSP accept that in politics, perception, suggestion and allegation can be as impactful as reality and, in fact, can be more dangerous?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Suggestions and allegations play on the minds of the electorate especially now that such a large proportion of our population has access to the Internet.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We further know that allegations have a way of continuing to colour impressions even after they had been disproved.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the various instances where a minority candidate had stood against a Chinese candidate in a SMC, the minority had won.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And there are some examples that Ms Poa had raised.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But let us just consider what if one of them had lost.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Would there have been suggestions, allegations and the perception that he or she had lost because of race?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would venture to say that inevitably, there would be such suggestions and the allegations and the perception of racialism and race-based voting by some.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And this could lead to racial unhappiness and distrust.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The current GRC system, in my view, does not even allow such perceptions to form.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I recall just a few days ago, that the hon Member Mr Leong had himself brought up how important perception is in politics.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He raised this in relation to various comments he had come across online regarding the rental of the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) properties.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, Mr Leong is probably keenly aware of the need to manage perceptions in politics.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My fourth question is: does the PSP accept that Singapore's racial and religious harmony is hard fought and precious but also fragile?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Does the PSP accept that even if we currently have some form of ethnic and religious modus vivendi, that this may change in the future?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I mentioned earlier that I would deal with the point on currency.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at the positions taken by all the political parties that I mentioned, they underscore their call for abolishing the GRC system on the fact that at this current point, Singaporeans are unlikely to vote based on race and that there is no evidence showing the same.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But inherent in the fact that they qualify that this is the current situation and hence, we should consider abolishing GRCs now, is an admission that it may not have been the same in the past, that things had changed over time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And this is the fundamental flaw in their argument.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If things can change for the better, they can also change for the worst.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And history, Sir, is rife with examples of people of different ethnicities, living next to each other peacefully for centuries and then, something happens, it is a small spark, a disagreement.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Countries have descended into civil war in this way.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have seen flashpoints of racial unease and tension arise from time to time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This was the trigger for my Adjournment Motion on racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even something that, for some, was simple and innocuous, like the use of a cut-out standee, was seen by others as evidence of insensitivity towards ethnic minorities or discrimination and lack of understanding.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A Government body was even accused of racism.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are allegations of Chinese privilege in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are uncles scolding interracial couples in the street.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These, Sir, are arguably small incidents, non-political matters that had, nonetheless, evoked significant feeling in minority communities as well as in the majority Chinese community.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further to the fact that all the calls for abolition of premise on current situation, they are also premised on likelihood.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: NSP uses the phrase "highly improbable"; WP's proposal is based on there being no evidence that voters vote solely on the basis of race, and "solely", of course, is in absolute term.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The underlying admission is that it could be one of the considerations but not the sole consideration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And PSP has proposed alternatives that admit that there is yet a concern because they are suggesting something else that will help to ameliorate the concern over minority representation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine this Motion is timed to coincide with the Presidential Elections where we may see an ethnic minority candidate pitted against one or more Chinese candidates, based just on the fact that several nomination forms were collected.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And this was referred to by Ms Poa.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Leong also dedicated a large proportion of his speech to the elected Presidency despite this Motion being about GRCs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But some have been saying that if Senior Minister Tharman, the minority candidate, wins, then this shows that the GRC system has become irrelevant because he had won against one or more Chinese candidates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think this is a fair or logical argument.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Senior Minister Tharman can only be described as a rather exceptional creature.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And Mr Murali was also mentioned but he had very considerable grassroots experience in Bukit Batok before he ran.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, these are exceptions and we should not use exceptions to make rules.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While we can aspire towards being blind to race, we should not be blind to the reality of ethnic feeling, especially those of minorities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The incidents I previously mentioned tested our unity and we must not dismiss the fact that racial politics is the fastest and most furious means to tear a society apart.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We may be idealistically thinking that we are beyond all these things now.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But we know that our racial unity is fragile.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think anybody would argue against this.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And we know that we must work hard to keep it together.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the event that it deteriorates for whatever reason – and we cannot discount this possibility – we must ensure that our structures of Government and elections are able to withstand changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The question is how should our institutions be built?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Fluffy, feel-good institutions that hope for the best of times or robust, resilient institutions that can withstand the worst?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, a fuss-free minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me full circle to my first point that there is no perfect electoral system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The natural question is whether we can work with what we have to tweak it such that the disadvantages are minimised while maintaining the good in the system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We should not throw away the baby with the bathwater.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And as Mr Leong mentioned, this has already happened.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Is this sufficient mitigation to the concerns that the PSP has raised about MPs sitting on the coat-tails of Ministers, voters voting on the "fear to lose" basis?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And these may be characterised more as political concerns, not social concerns of which the GRC system was built.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This call to abolish the GRC system is premised on these very same ideas that Singaporeans have moved beyond race; that in voting, we will consider every candidate only on the relevant merits and be more or less blind to race.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It also expects that in a situation where a minority candidate loses, as inevitably one eventually will, there will be little or no perception that race did not contribute to that loss.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What if we have a troublemaker intent on using race to gain political advantage within the electoral system?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: GRCs are unique to Singapore's electoral landscape and require political parties to field candidates from different races in the GRC team to ensure that minority representation in Parliament is upheld.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This system helps to promote inter-ethnic understanding and cooperation, enabling minority candidates to be elected to Parliament and ensuring that their voices are heard at the national level.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The GRC plays an important role in maintaining Singapore's social fabric and promoting racial harmony, which is critical in a diverse nation like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And this is why I cannot support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to raise three points on GRCs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This would increase the competition and diversity in elections.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: By reducing the size of GRCs, it is easier for Opposition parties to field credible candidates to contest every seat and could lead to greater voter choice and accountability for elected officials.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, reducing the size of GRCs could help to promote greater representation of minority groups and communities in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's population is increasing and the needs of Singaporeans have also increased.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I would encourage the Government to continue to increase the number of Parliamentarians in Parliament to increase the diversity in the discussions here today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, another area where GRCs can be improved is in terms of diversity.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The Elections Department of Singapore requires a minimum of one MP representing a minority racial community in a GRC.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: While GRCs aim to achieve minority representation in Parliament, there should also be diversity in terms of gender representation as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, Singapore is a democratic society, and the power rests with the voters, who should decide who represents them in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: All politicians should earn their votes by convincing voters that they are the best candidates to represent Singaporeans' interests and values.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This involves engaging with voters, listening to their concerns and communicating a clear vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This goes for every Member here – PAP, WP, PSP or not.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Whether this view has merit or not, reducing the number of representatives in a GRC could increase the power of the electorate and enable Singaporeans to hold their elected representatives accountable.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is important for Parliamentarians to be accountable to their constituents and to work hard to earn their trust and support.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This means being transparent about their actions and decisions, seeking feedback from voters, and working collaboratively with their stakeholders to achieve common goals.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Like what my fellow NMP Raj Joshua Thomas has mentioned, the PSP must understand that there is no perfect system and we should be striving for the best system for Singapore and Singaporeans today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial to consider the potential impacts of abolishing GRCs before making any changes to the electoral system.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Any changes made should promote greater diversity and inclusivity in political representation and not inadvertently lead to a reduction in representation for minorities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To I start off, I stand not in support of the Motion, but I thank Mr Leong, as always, giving me homework to do.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Because of this Motion, I must admit that I learned a lot more about GRCs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: According to Singapore InfoPedia, the setting up of GRCs was to ensure that Singapore’s Parliament would always be multiracial in composition and representation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The constitution stipulates that teams for candidates standing for election in a GRC must include at least one member from a minority community.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: GRCs were put into practice in the 1988 General Elections.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To understand better, I researched to understand the history of GRCs-in-the-making.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The issue of ensuring minority ethnic representation in Parliament was first raised by then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew in July 1982.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to the concept of GRC, which was then termed the "Team MP" concept, there were actually different proposals raised by both PAP and Opposition parties at that time, which included “twin constituencies”, “giving minority voters extra vote”, “communal based constituencies”, “dividing Parliament along communal lines” and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In an article that summarised the history of the making the GRC, it was said that the GRC concept was fleshed out after a long-drawn debate which included representations made to a Parliamentary Select Committee.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Committee was set up to investigate public support for the scheme and see if there was a better proposal to ensure multiracial representation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was a controversial issue as race was openly discussed for the first time at that time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was controversial as critics saw it as a ploy to handicap the diminutive Opposition further at that time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There were two issues debated: the first is with regard to the principle of ensuring that Parliament is multiracial in composition because Singapore is a multiracial society; and the second is with regard to the “how to achieve it”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first issue was agreed to unanimously in the House, including opposition Members of Parliament at that time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The second issue of “how” was of course, hotly debated.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Like already discussed by my fellow NMPs, the GRC while not perfect, was decided to have the best chance to ensure that Singapore’s Parliament would always be multiracial in composition and representation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty-five years on, has the GRC delivered on its promise?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, 19.5%, today we have 28.3%, considering I am not even going to talk about all the positives, the achievements, and the growth that Singapore has experienced and attained in the last 35 years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, is the GRC concept still relevant today?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong in his Second Reading speech in January 1988 to move the Bill to implement GRCs, said, “this Bill is to ensure the long-term political stability of Singapore in two ways: first by ensuring that Parliament will always be multiracial and representative of our society; and second by encouraging the practice of multiracial politics by all political parties.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is a multiracial, multi-religious society, but not by chance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For Singaporeans to enjoy racial and religious harmony, the PAP and the Government consider multiracialism to be a fundamental axiom of politics in Singapore.” These words still ring true today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps even more so today as the world is becoming more polarised and social media content carrying falsehoods and rhetoric that are not helpful for building cohesive societies, is everywhere.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Closer to home, we might recall the sad incident of a lecturer, Mr Tan, who made racist remarks against an interracial couple, and had to be taken to task.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One might say that this was just an incident.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But we must face the realities that Singapore is not homogenous, and our multiracial harmony must not be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Well, I added another question to my three questions, because I was just analysing, I have no recommendations for anybody.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is this whole big thing about a conspiracy theory that GRCs was a ploy by the PAP to handicap the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The results of the GE 2011 and then GE 2020 should put any conspiracy theory to bed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the GRC concept, all the political parties need to have the gravitas to be able to attract a strong diverse slate of men and women that reflects multiracial Singapore; to contest in elections on a multiracial platform and not with communal or racial undertone; and when they win, be part of a multiracial Parliament that represents our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, it looks like the key issue is perhaps the size of the GRC and the number of SMCs, which I am sure the Government is listening very carefully to and will make the right call.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For me, before I close, if you may indulge me as I share a few thoughts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I say this not only for politicians, but actually for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not mess it up for our children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, Parliament is serious business of governing a country.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We will always be a work in progress and we cannot take it for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do recognise though that there will always be a group of young Singaporeans who will be reaching the age of majority to vote in the next GE.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Naturally, they would not have had the chance to follow the debate that led to the implementation of this GRC system some 35 years ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I do see some utility in having this topic raised here, once again, in this House to provide our younger voters an opportunity to appreciate the reasons for the system and the arguments presented on both sides of the aisle as to whether the system continues to be fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For that reason, I thank the hon NCMPs, Ms Poa and Mr Leong, for providing me with the chance to speak on this Motion standing in their names.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will draw from my own experience in standing for elections as a PAP candidate in an SMC as well as in a GRC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before I do so, I would like to make three preliminary points.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, based on the speeches that I have heard thus far, I assume that all in this House are united in the wish to see adequate representation of minority races in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, on the quintessential matter of managing race relations, the preferred approach of the Government must be to deal with the facts as they are.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where the assessment is that race continues to matter in our society, the approach of the Government cannot be to blithely ignore it but to address the issue head on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that the then hon MP, Mr Chiam See Tong, who was often referred to as a doyen amongst Opposition MPs, agreed to in the Select Committee hearing on the GRC system in 1988.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third and finally, I accept that the GRC system has its shortcomings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, in my research, I noted that the Government, when it introduced the GRC system in this House, also candidly acknowledged that it is not a perfect system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One shortcoming perceived among political observers and academics is that the GRC system requires minority representation at the point of elections but not during the subsistence or the tenure of MPs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that has been settled by the highest Court of our land in interpreting the legal provisions setting up the GRC system in 1988.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The explanation of the Government that was expressly noted by the Court is that the system must ensure that the candidates from the minority race should not be able to hold the other candidates in the team to ransom to force a re-election.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that the hon NCMP, Ms Poa, raised in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst there is logic in the reasoning, I do accept, as she did, that not all fellow Singaporeans feel comfortable with it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ms Poa came up with two ideas – the equivalent of the NCMP system as well as a Parliament based on proportional system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She suggested that there is no need to rush with the consideration of these ideas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first, it does by ensuring minority representation; and the second, it does by removing the leverages of communal politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To illustrate, I now turn to my personal experience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To my knowledge, I am the second minority candidate that the PAP fielded in an SMC since the implementation of the GRC system in 1988.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When I stood for elections in the 2016 by-election at Bukit Batok SMC, I was not exactly a newbie.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had the privilege of serving in Bukit Batok as a community leader and a PAP branch activist for about 16 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My mentor was the late Dr Ong Chit Chung, then MP for Bukit Batok between 1988 and 2008 when he passed away.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: During the three years after he passed away, between 2008 and 2011, when the next GE was held, I worked very closely with our community leaders to hold things together at our constituency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, by 2016, I managed to get some political experience under my belt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Between 2011 and 2015, I served as the Branch Chairman of the PAP Paya Lebar Branch.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my capacity as Branch Chairman, I gained a tremendous amount of experience in leading both political and community outreach programmes for the benefit of residents there.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also stood for elections as part of a team of five in Aljunied GRC in GE 2015.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We lost the elections but gained much in terms of practical experience and insights.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, even though I was going into the 2016 by-election as a first-time candidate at an SMC, I had some lines of experience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the result, the people of Bukit Batok voted me in as their MP in May 2016.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would highlight that during the campaign, I had to address the very fair point as to whether, being not conversant in Mandarin, I would be able to engage Mandarin-speaking residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I did not see this as a racial issue but a practical one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciated that Mandarin-speaking residents would naturally be concerned that if I am not able to understand them, I would have difficulty in representing their interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As it turned out, I was able to convince my constituents that I would work harder to overcome the language barrier with my team of volunteers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It also helped that I could hold a simple conversation in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By the time of the 2020 GE, the PAP decided to field me again at Bukit Batok SMC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As an incumbent candidate, I had established a record of service which I put forth before my constituents for their consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had a tough election battle in GE 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To me, I read it as the constituents of Bukit Batok acknowledging that, overall, having regard to my character, record and experience, the fact that I was from a minority race was not an issue to them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To some, this may seem to argue that we do not need the GRC system, since a minority candidate can win an SMC of majority Chinese.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was something that Ms Poa alluded to in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They may also quote Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam who led his team to secure the highest levels of support in a GRC in GEs twice – also something raised in the debate today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They may say that voters are fair-minded, can see beyond race and we should respect this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But having said that, Iet me show you the realpolitik on the ground – attempts to politicise race issues during both campaigns at Bukit Batok SMC which, thankfully, failed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Lee said, "it is not unknown for racial sentiments to emerge and be exploited during election campaign." In particular, he said that he came across comments in the social media making the point about race in "quite an open way." During a press interview on the same day, I frankly acknowledged that race issues are present in our society but expressed my confidence that I can overcome these issues with my team.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As they say, a picture speaks a thousand words.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The LED screens show a blown-up photo of a flyer used in my campaign in GE 2020 that was defaced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I think hon Members looking at this slide will straightway appreciate the racial undertones quite quickly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I got this photo from a resident who was upset about the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She pointed out to me that there was a Chinese character written over my chest which was partially hidden through colouring over the character.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: When I had occasion to review the photo whilst drafting this speech, I realised the same character was written on both hands, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: How Indian must I be to be oblivious to a Chinese calling for my death?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And yet, perhaps fortunately, how Singaporean can I be to get the job done and meet my key performance indicators (KPIs)?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: When I saw the attempts to politicise the elections on racial lines, I made a decision not to be distracted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I focused on what I believed were the priorities of my constituents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hon Members would recall that at the Opening of this Session of Parliament following GE 2020, I said that all of us in politics must grow the skin of a rhino and the heart of a lion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: When I stood for elections in Aljunied GRC in 2015, I certainly did not see similar attempts at racial politicisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I personally think that the reason for this is attributable to the fact that I stood as part of a team in a GRC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It would be difficult for any person to exploit matters along racial lines during elections when the political parties in the contest fielded minority candidates in their respective teams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In a GRC fight, we are in it together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The GRC is a compound, not a mixture that can pried away, one element from another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I pointed out that I was not a newbie.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, even then, I faced coordinated attempts to politicise the campaign along racial lines, which were rebuffed by Bukit Batok voters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thankfully, I had thick skin and I was able to focus on my campaign.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: About a week ago, I shared with my elder daughter, a teenager, that I will be speaking on race issues in connection with this Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In response, she told me that during the 2020 hustings – she would have been in primary school then – she came across an outright racist remark about me on Twitter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She, however, decided not to tell me about it because she felt that I was already going through a tough election.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She was protecting me at a time when actually it is the father's duty to protect the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I looked at her carefully when she told me this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She had a habit of biting her lips when she was upset.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She is now at peace, although she had to grow up much faster as a result.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I ask hon Members from the majority race in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Imagine that you are from a minority race.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Would you want to put your own son or daughter through an election in a situation where there is a good probability that your child may be excoriated simply on account of his or her race?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They will not be prepared to be made fun of along racial lines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We have made progress from the days of race riots, but we need to be honest and realistic about race relations always.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I can speak simple Mandarin, I can have political experience, I can rise above racial needling, but after all this, let us be honest, I am still “too Indian” for some voters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There may be a time when race may not matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Because in a GRC, you are not going to go up against any particular race, but a coalition of us, bound together by the collective interests of the GRC and of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Each of us is constitutive of this group, this compound that forms a protective coating against racial attacks, from wherever they come, and against any of us from any race.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Only then, we can hope to succeed, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But perhaps, I should just clarify before I stray out of order, that this Motion calls for the abolition of the GRC, and not about the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because I appreciate Ms Hazel Poa's various ideas and suggestions, but I was a bit confused by Mr Leong's speech that spent the greater bulk of his comment on the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, if I stick narrowly to the Motion, I think I should confine my comments to the debate on the GRC today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I would also like to thank Mr Murali for sharing his very personal experiences and reflections.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The question is: do we, as a people and as a system, believe in ensuring that the Parliament, our highest legislative body of the land, is representative of a multiracial Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Or, as Mr Raj Joshua Thomas said, are we willing to take the risk of rule by majority without safeguards for our minority communities, without safeguards against racial politics that can easily tear apart the fabric of our nation?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are the fundamental issues in discussing this Motion and it forms the basis of why we have the GRCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I ask all Members of this House to carefully consider this when we vote on the Motion later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members have also given their views on the design of the GRC system, such as the sizes and number of GRCs that we should have.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will address these issues in my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is the principle of the GRC system that is at stake here today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will always seek to develop models, and we must always seek to develop models that best meet our needs and circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When Independence was thrust upon us, we could easily have chosen to organise ourselves based on majoritarian rule.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, since Independence, we have always been sensitive to the needs of our minorities, especially for the majority to exercise greater responsibility to ensure that the rights and interests of our minorities are not neglected.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In our Constitution, we recognise and safeguard the special position of the Malays as the indigenous people of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
