text: We also clearly state, “It shall be the responsibility of the Government constantly to care for the interests of the racial and religious minorities in Singapore”.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We prohibited discrimination against citizens on the grounds of race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We instituted the Presidential Council for Minority Rights, or PCMR in short, to ensure that new laws passed by Parliament do not prejudice any racial or religious community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We put in place guardrails because we value multiracialism.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The GRC system is an extension of this philosophy – to minimise the risk that this House no longer represents our multiracial demography and ride roughshod over the interests of our minority communities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This means we minimise the risk that any party can try to win votes by playing the race card.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Poa’s alternative suggestions of minority NCMP and proportional representation do not address this point and I will come back to explain this in a while.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This issue matters, especially in hotly contested seats where an appeal to race could shape the outcome of a contest.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is very real, as the hon Member for Bukit Batok had just shared.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This matters and will continue to matter, even if a GRC loses its minority Member, through illness or resignation, during the Parliamentary term.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because any party that wants to be re-elected will know the importance of winning the support of all races.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is an important safeguard to prevent our politics from becoming racial.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, contrary to what was claimed by Ms Poa, the GRC system does not divide us by race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, it is designed to disincentivise the appeal of race in politics to minimise the chances and leverage that people can use race in an electoral contest.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Those are the core issues and the fundamental issues.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First is the claim that GRCs unfairly benefit the incumbent by tapping on the “star power” in each team.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Otherwise, in Ms Poa's words, it is known as the “coat-tail” argument.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I do not think that “star power” is the preserve of the incumbent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One can argue that the “star power” of Mr Low Thia Khiang would have contributed much to the Workers’ Party’s electoral success in Aljunied in 2011.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Likewise, maybe you would also agree with me that few would deny that the “star power” of Dr Tan Cheng Bock has contributed much to PSP's showing in West Coast in 2020, leading to both Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa being the two NCMPs in our House today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Conversely, the “star power” can cut the other way.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Should a member of the team, Minister or otherwise, become a liability, he or she can also affect the electoral performance of the entire team to the team’s detriment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Various Members have suggested for the GRC size to be smaller or having more SMCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I want everyone to know that the Government understands the sentiments of our people, and I am sure the Electoral Boundaries Review Committee (EBRC) here can appreciate the aspirations of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not for the Government of the day to decide, as suggested by Mr Leong.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Government of the day has made clear our position.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong has made clear our position.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And it is the collective decision of the Government of the day, not any particular individual and not whether is it Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong or otherwise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, I want to touch on this other point, which is related to the size and shape of the electoral division.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Leong suggested that every of our divisions is rather homogenous in its characteristics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The question is: are we better served if our divisions are not microcosms of the country but, instead, across our island, we have divisions that have very unique and skewed characteristics, and maybe even along racial lines?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If so, what kind of outcomes do we expect from such electoral contests?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The reason and the advantage of all divisions being microcosms – plus or minus a bit – of the national characteristics allows everyone to focus our selection of the candidates to represent them based on our collective national interest, and not on sectoral characteristics or interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In other countries, they have gone exactly that way, where electoral contests are fought on narrow sectoral interests or characteristics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It does not detract from the underlying fundamental reasons of having the GRC system to ensure that our Parliament remains multiracial and our politics non-racial.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third is on the need to call a by-election to fill a position vacated by a minority or any other Member.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This has been debated and clarified in this House and I will not repeat all the arguments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Courts have settled the law on this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members may wish to refer to the 2017 High Court decision to dismiss the application filed by Dr Wong Souk Yee for a by-election to be held in Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC after Mdm Halimah Yacob resigned her seat as Member of Parliament to stand for the Presidential Election.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Dr Wong subsequently filed an appeal over the ruling.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, the Court of Appeal ruled that there was no requirement for a by-election to be called in Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC after Mdm Halimah Yacob resigned her seat as Member of Parliament to stand for the Presidential Election.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In a GRC contest, the voters vote for the team and it is the GRC team that represents the GRC and all its constituents in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Not requiring a by-election to fill the position vacated by a minority or any other Member is to prevent any single team member holding the rest to ransom by threatening to step down, as Members have also pointed out.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This also does not detract from the fact that no one can hope to gain electoral advantage by playing on race, as the team would still be required to be multiracial in their approach and advocacy of Singaporeans' interests to appeal to all races in the next election.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fourth, the claim that the GRC system has stunted the growth of the Opposition.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As Mr Leong pointed out, before the introduction of the GRC system, we had only two Opposition Members in 1984.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If PSP truly believes that the GRC system disadvantages you, then I find it odd that you sent 19 of your 24 candidates to contest in four GRCs in the most recent GE, instead of contesting in all the SMCs possible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Unless the constraint was due to the inability to attract sufficient quality minority candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If so, then this is precisely what the GRC system seeks to do – prevent single-race party campaigning along racial lines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fifth, why not have other forms of proportional representation system to ensure minority representation in this House, as suggested by Ms Poa?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This issue has been debated extensively in this House, and I will, again, not repeat all the arguments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members may wish to refer to the Hansard, in particular the speech by the Prime Minister on 27 January 2016, during the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some parties will be incentivised to build their base around a particular interest in order to win seats, rather than to appeal to a broad majority of voters.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Poa also suggested having an NCMP scheme for minorities, so that minority candidates who lost the contest in SMCs but have the highest percentage of votes can be appointed as NCMPs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But unfortunately, I do not think it will achieve our objectives of ensuring Parliament is multiracial and minimising the chances of candidates and parties playing the race card.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, if we only have SMCs, there is no guarantee that there will even be enough minority candidates among the losing candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we only have SMCs, there is no guarantee that we will even have enough minority candidates among the losing candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, more importantly, the NCMP system comes into play when the ruling party has a large majority in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: By Ms Hazel's suggestion, it will come into play when the ruling party has a large majority without minority Members, or with very few minority Members.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our political divide will be along racial lines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And this, if I may suggest, will be most dangerous for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Various Opposition Members have also previously criticised the NCMP scheme as being a second-class MP scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If this is true, can we imagine a situation where the minorities are all or largely in the NCMPs or party list as a group, while the rest or a vast majority of the elected MPs being the racial majority?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Is this a better outcome for us in this House?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I have thought deeply about your suggestions, but unfortunately, I do not think it will solve our problems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If not, it will complicate things even more.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At the beginning of my speech, I highlighted the twin objectives of the GRC system, and they bear reminding – one, to ensure that our Parliament will always be representative of the racial make-up of our society; and two, to ensure that our politics do not become racially charged.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These two objectives are equally important and Ms Poa's suggestions will unfortunately not ensure that our politics do not become racially charged.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: PSP made the argument that we should move beyond race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And Workers' Party (WP) says that "we are confident that Singaporeans do not vote solely on race".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I am sure Singaporeans do not vote solely on the basis of race, but that is not the question before us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The question before us is: "should race be a critical factor in their decision, even if it is not the only factor?" And to PSP's and some other Opposition suggestions that we should move beyond race, we all agree with this aspiration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I am sure I have the support of every Member of this House to support this, that we all aspire to move beyond race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, I will be the first to aspire to the day where we have a Singaporean tribe, regardless of race, language and religion, that we have all gone beyond race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We recite it in our pledge every day – "We, the citizens of Singapore, pledge ourselves as one united people, regardless of race, language or religion".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One united people, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But having an aspiration is not the same as it being a reality today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members may wish to revisit the exchange recorded in the Hansard between the late-Mr Lee Kuan Yew and then-NMP Mr Viswa Sadasivan on this issue on 19 August 2009, as referenced by Mr Raj Joshua Thomas in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This was the speech where many of us learned the phrase "highfalutin".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I will personally be very careful and not ignore the realities that we are still confronting today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many Members have shared your own personal stories.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even if there are a few bad hats, they do not represent us as a people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But indeed, what we have been dealing with is the GRC system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And the coincidences are quite uncanny and not just the last decade, but I referred to the table that Mr Low put forward in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Every constituency, where there is a tight fight between the PAP and WP, what happens?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, until we can have some assurance from the PAP, will you stop using the GRC for this purpose?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The accusations of gerrymandering happen in every country where the electoral boundaries are being drawn or redrawn.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Gerrymandering goes back 200 years or more in the US; what we consider the paragon of democracy today.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And those accusations are still being made for gerrymandering.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, it is not an issue of whether it is a GRC or an SMC.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, I think as Mr Leong or Ms Hazel Poa has pointed out, it is those GRCs or those constituencies that have been won by the Opposition where it has not been changed at all.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I do not understand why the EBRC has not changed them, but perhaps, you can make a request for them all to become SMCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Number one, WP is prepared to contest any constituency on an SMC basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is our position in the manifesto, we have laid it out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We went to elections in 2020 with that in our manifesto.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It just tells you this constituency, this number, that is, it was this number; now, it is this number, this is the new boundary, finished.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, you are going to continue to have cynicism about the GRC system and it is not going to stop.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Insofar as this Motion is concerned, I think we have laid our position out quite evidently.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have given my views on where the GRC system has been helpful for society and I think it is important for me to state that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it would be remiss of me not to highlight to the public and to Singaporeans at large, why the WP takes the position that it does.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I am mindful that your colleague has the final right of reply and she is down for a 40-minute speech.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, I ask for the clarification to be short, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Just to answer Minister Chan's question, first of all, the first point you made about the minority representation, taking this factor out of the politics, on all these, in this House, I think all of us are all aligned.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is no different between PAP and PSP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: On the second point, I was trying to give you an examination question, but I think you failed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In 1980s, just now I mentioned, it was a very significant period for Singapore politics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because in 1981, Mr JB Jeyaratnam won the by-election.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Before that, from 1968 to 1981, it was 100% PAP representation in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, as a student, when we read the newspaper and we listened to Mr Lee Kuan Yew's views and all that, it came right in and today, I would not forget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I quote, from Mr Lee Kuan Yew, 1984, "One man, one vote is a most difficult form of government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: From time to time, the results can be erratic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They get bored with stable, steady improvements in life and in a reckless moment, they vote for a change for change’s sake."

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think he is making a fresh speech.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It has nothing to do with clarification on the Minister's speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: No, no, no; I am asking the Minister whether he knows some of the thinking —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong, let me deal with Mr Lim's point.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I will allow you to go on for a little longer but please ask your question.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think this derives from your second point from your previous clarification where you were asking Minister Chan essentially to guess what was in your mind.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Now, you are sharing what is in your mind with a quote from Mr Lee.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, after that quote, please, then put your question to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is due to his reservation also – maybe, say, 50-50 – of the one man, one vote system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is why, put it under the group voting, vote as a group and not one man, one vote.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think Minister Chan understands your question that whether or not it remains a one man-one vote; or one lady-one-vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I remember that was what Mr Lee said.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let us bring it back to this Motion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Was that the only reason that Mr Lee talked about the GRC system?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Was Mr Lee not expressing this in a wider context of how we formed governments?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think, first point, please do not take things out of context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There was a context why Mr Lee said what he said.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And what he said, I personally think was valid and I will come to that in a while.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But that has nothing to do with today's Motion about the GRC and minority representation because what you have just highlighted was that, yes, Mr Lee was concerned about the stability and the effectiveness of any government system, especially for a small country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I will share with you my own views, having been in the Government, or served in the Government in various capacities all these years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is there a reason for us to think very hard about the kind of governance system we want, be it democracy, or whatever else people call us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Or even democracy, or the variants of democracy that the world practises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It goes back down to two points, if I may say so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, are we prepared to find our own solutions for our own problems and challenges, or do we just copy?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if we just copy, who do we copy from?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And let us be frank, whether those systems that we intend to copy from have produced better outcomes than ours?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do not profess that we have found the perfect system and we have delivered the perfect solutions for Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But is this better than other alternatives that have been considered?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is to paraphrase Winston Churchill: democracy may be the worst form of governance except for all else that have been tried.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the first question for us is – are we prepared to evolve our own system according to our needs, or do we just copy?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if we just copy, please tell us why copying another system will serve our needs better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, and this is my heartfelt response to Mr Leong, I have noticed very often in this House that we bring to this House various ideas from other jurisdictions and countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is part of our DNA to never be satisfied with our own system, but to constantly seek improvement – because we want to defy the odds of history for Singapore to be around for as long as possible, for us to have enough time to evolve into what I call the Singaporean Tribe, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I have never believed that just by copying other people, we will be exceptional, or we can distinguish ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When I was in junior college, I walked the opposite way that Minister Shanmugam said the other day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He walked out of East Sussex Lane from Ghim Moh Road to Holland Road to take a bus.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I alighted at Ghim Moh Road and walked along East Sussex Lane, scrambled down the railway track to Raffles Junior College at Ghim Moh Road.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: My friends would know that generally, I walk quite fast.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And since that time, coming from a different family background, to say the least, I have told myself that I would never be able to compete with other people if I were to just follow them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not have the means and I may not have all their strengths.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For me to compete, I must distinguish myself in my own ways.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every morning, when I walked down East Sussex Lane, I reminded myself of it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have a saying: 跟潮流就是走在潮流的后端; to follow the tide is to follow and be a follower always.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not want my country to just follow other people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want my country and my people to stand tall because we are bold enough to know what our challenges are and come up with solutions for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I know we are responsible enough to not try and do experiments, but to consider things seriously.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All of us here will agree that it has served us well, but it has its own flaws as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When we want to do something, there will always be suggestions, protests or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But do we not do it just because of what this generation says?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Or do we not do it because it does not benefit the next generation?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you ask me, is democracy perfect, I will tell you that it is not the perfect system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And so, if I put that in the context of what Mr Lee said, that is a wider context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The wider context is: how do we govern a small country with a short history, with no natural hinterland or resources except our people?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we distinguish ourselves, find our relevance, find our own solutions, and make sure that we take care of people, not just in this generation, but in future generations?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we evolve a system of government whereby people elected here will think seriously, not just about our generation, but also about future generations?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: After all that has been said, I think it is quite clear that there is no disagreement on the importance of multiracial representation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Where we defer is simply on how to achieve that multiracial representation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I disagree with Minister Chan when he said that our proposals do not ensure multiracial representation or prevent race-based parties.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Earlier on, when I spoke about proportional representation, I mentioned this only briefly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Perhaps that could be the reason why it was not clearly conveyed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, let me go into further details now.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Typically, in a hybrid electoral system, which is the one that we suggested, containing both elements of first-past-the-post and proportional representation, each voter has two ballots instead of one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The first ballot is to vote for a candidate in a local SMC and the candidate with the most votes is elected.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, this should address the hon Member Raj Joshua Thomas' concern about the geographical link between MPs and their residents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The second ballot will then be to vote for a party at the national level and the seats are allocated to each party based on their national vote share.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Each party typically has a party list of the candidates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, if a party is allocated 10 seats, usually the first 10 candidates on the party list get elected.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But I am not suggesting that we copy wholesale the system that is in place in other countries, unlike what Minister Chan is suggesting.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am suggesting that we adapt such a system to meet our needs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, how can we adapt this to ensure minority representation?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Up to three in five must have a Malay candidate, while the other two must be Indian or others.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is analogous to the Ethnic Integration Policy quota in Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: These requirements can be limited to only parties that contest in more than one seat.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is to make room for independent candidates in our electoral system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, by imposing these racial quotas similar to the way it is done in HDB flats, we can ensure that parties are multiracial, and they do not play race-based politics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Another comment earlier about proportional representation is the fear of a fragmented parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: A common feature in proportional representation is actually a threshold.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Only political parties that obtain a minimum national vote percentage are allocated seats proportionally.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This feature serves to screen out the parties with extreme positions and insufficient electoral support that prevents parliament from getting too fragmented.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The ballot on party list is like a national level multi-cornered fight with participation from all the political parties that wish to contest.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If the results of past multi-cornered fights in Singapore elections is any guide, we are unlikely to see too fragmented a parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Minister Chan earlier mentioned that the fear is that a proportional representation system would result in race-based politics and also parties that run on minority interests.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I have addressed the point about race-based politics and now on minority interests.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I do not see that that is necessarily a bad thing for there to be parties with minority interests.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: For example, green parties have always had some minority support.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Environmental concerns have now become mainstream but green parties still face great difficulties in winning elections under a first-past-the-post system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, incorporating some level of proportional representation into an electoral system will ensure that minority concerns are also represented and that can only be beneficial to our decision-making.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: When a political party enjoys clear majority support, a first-past-the-post system tends to give that party more seats in Parliament than its national vote share.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But when political support is more divided, the outcome becomes more volatile.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As an illustration, consider the other side of the coin.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In other words, a drop of 20% in national support level can result in a drop of 80% in seats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Of course, national support level does not normally drop 20% that quickly or that easily.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This illustration merely seeks to point out that the volatility and unpredictability of election outcomes under the first-past-the-post system when support level hovers around 50%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: At this stage, a proportional representation system actually brings greater stability and predictability.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Next, I will move on to the issues relating to the NCMP suggestion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As I have mentioned before, we are confident that our minority candidates can stand on their own and win elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Because we also agree with the importance of multiracial representation in Parliament, that is why we also proposed two alternatives to ensure that.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The beauty of the NCMP scheme is that it does not kick in when it is not needed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But if it is needed, if not enough minority candidates can win on their own, then we need to know why and address the underlying issues head on instead of sweeping them under the GRC carpet.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Racism exists in all spheres, not only during elections.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: At this point, I actually have a question to ask of Minister Chan.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I did not quite understand why he said that if we adopt this scheme, that all the minorities will be NCMPs in Opposition and the ruling party MPs will be the Chinese majority.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Under this NCMP scheme, the NCMP can be from either party, whether the ruling party or the Opposition – unlike the current NCMP scheme, which is just for the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Mr Murali Pillai also weighed in with his personal experience, citing examples of the kind of experience he had running his campaign and experiencing attempts by people who exploit the race card.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: To totally eradicate it is probably not practical, even though we would all try our best to minimise that as far as possible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But I think the point is that they did not succeed, even though they tried to play the race card.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Even though racism does exist, it is not to the extent that it actually affects election outcomes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The hon Member Janet Ang mentioned that an article or report from IPS, I think, in 2013 about the fact that Opposition parties also similarly benefit from GRCs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: That was after the Workers' Party (WP) managed to win Aljunied GRC.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I think Minister Chan similarly made the point as well that the WP and the PSP also benefited from the coat tail effect and, specifically, that I also benefited from it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I think the question here is whether GRCs are the right way and the best way for Singapore, and not whether I personally benefited from it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The doubt is raised by Ms Janet Ang over the Opposition's claim that GRCs have had a detrimental effect on the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Allow me to quote statistics from our GEs around the time when the legislation was changed to introduce the GRC and to make further amendments to it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As I mentioned earlier, it was done over three amendments in 1988, 1991 and 1996.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: To recap briefly, in 1988, the three-member GRC was introduced and justified on the basis of minority representation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In 1991 and 1997, the sizes of GRC were increased and the total number of GRC seats, the upper limit, was increased.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Let us look at the effect these amendments had on our minority representation and political development in the GEs following these changes, which were GE 1988, GE 1991 and GE 1997.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In the next two GEs, minority MPs made up 21% and 22.9% respectively.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In contrast, its effect on our political development is more dramatic.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In GE 1984, before the introduction of GRCs, 38% of the seats were uncontested.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: After three amendments, the real effect of the GRC system is this.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: It made hardly any difference to minority representation but led to a huge increase in walkovers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Faced with raised hurdles, which is the GRC, Opposition parties had to adopt a by-election strategy in response.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Looking at these figures, it behoves us to revisit these questions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This happened naturally as part of society's development, similar to the way women's representation in Parliament increased to 30% without any GRC-like intervention.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The justification that this is done so that we need not change the boundaries so frequently is unconvincing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am sure we have all heard jokes about how residents keep changing constituencies in each election without moving house.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Would not the same be achieved by a few SMCs working together?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Thirdly, why were the upper limit on GRC seats increased?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Is it a coincidence that as these changes were made, the number of walkovers increased dramatically?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In the recent GE, the PAP has tried to make the GRC smaller.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Six-member GRCs were removed and the average size of GRCs were reduced just slightly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: However, as long as GRCs remain, so too remain the problems associated with the GRC system, namely, the coat tail effect, reduced voter influence on outcome, the hampering of political development, and underserved and under-represented residents in GRCs with unfilled vacancies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The PAP has mentioned before that even though there is a vacancy in the GRC, residents are happy with the arrangements that they have made for the other MPs to cover the duties of the MP who has left.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In fact, residents have never been directly asked if they preferred a GRC or SMC system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If the PAP is certain of this, would it be willing to ask this question to voters, using the Presidential Election as the means to conduct a referendum?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am sure this is a question that many Singaporeans would want a say in.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Who better to decide how voters should be represented than the voters themselves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Minister Chan earlier spoke about the by-election and concluded by saying that the Court has decided.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In the past, Singapore has benefited from a strong single-party system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: At our developmental stages, many countries were ahead of us in development and provided us many examples with which to study.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We could emulate where appropriate and discard where not.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This can erode democratic principles and perpetuate a culture of nepotism or cronyism.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Checks and balances are necessary for the longer term.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Singapore has entered a different stage of development.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: With each GE, the growing desire of the voters for greater checks and balances and political diversity becomes more apparent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As we move towards a more balanced political landscape, many changes will be needed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There were a couple of clarifications that Ms Hazel Poa asked of me.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will not go through point by point, given the time, but can I just make the following few points in response to her questions?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, I think as a generic point, it would be good for the PSP to at least lay out their whole proposal at the beginning of the debate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am not sure those details that you just presented were a response to my comments or you already had them worked out all before.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If I may humbly suggest that if you have got it all worked out before, I think it is good for us to debate the details and know the details right from the onset instead of having it in the concluding speech because then we might have to revisit many of these issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the spirit of me taking an examination today, you said that we can have Party A, B, and C, making sure that their slate of candidates has X or Y number of minority candidates to make sure that there will be representation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, can I just put it this way?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Party A fields a Chinese here, Party B fields a Malay there, and Party C fields an Indian there.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Does it mean that it will guarantee minority representation?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You mentioned this two-vote system: vote once for the first-past-the-post and one for the proportional representation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Once you have this, there will be a tendency and we cannot escape from the tendency that when you want to win the vote on the proportional representation, go on the sectoral interest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Each and every one of us will have our pet topic that we may be happy or unhappy with this Government or whichever government we want to have, but what serves our interests best?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For those countries that have proportional representation, yes, you have many parties representing many groups all on the sectoral basis.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Have they become more effective in mobilising national action, whereby people are prepared to give trade-offs and consider it holistically whereby parties have to internalise the trade-offs within themselves, or is every party going to the Parliament just to contest on the basis of their narrow sectoral interests and end up with horse trading?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is that the kind of system that will allow us to have the strong and decisive government that you say that is required for us to distinguish ourselves as a nation?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You mentioned – this is new to me – that the NCMP will also apply to the Ruling Party.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, the NCMP scheme does not apply to the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the NCMP scheme applies to the ruling party, then it is essentially called a party list.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, you just reconsider what I just said in the second point – is the party list a mechanism that will not polarise us and end up with people running on single issues?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That the ruling party shall also be entitled to NCMP, which I think, boils down to a party list.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And finally, can I just make one plea to PSP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think we already have enough challenges trying to make sure that we have a clear Presidential Election if it is to be contested and to help Singaporeans understand the role of the Elected Presidency as we have designed it into our system – as the Head of State, as the custodian of our Reserves, Public Service appointments,	 and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Please do not confuse the issue and suggest that we turn the Elected Presidency into a referendum on the GRC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not see how this serves our democracy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have enough challenges trying to get everyone to come on board, understand the role of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not a check on the Government, it is not an Opposition party; it is the custodian of our Reserves and the Head of State for us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not a referendum for the GRC, to say the least.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: First, let me address the issue about the NCMP suggestion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In our proposal, what we said was that if we do not have enough minority candidates elected, then the NCMP for minorities will be chosen from those with the highest percentage of votes, no restriction on party.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, just those with the highest votes; it could be the ruling party, or it could be the Opposition party.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In our proposal, I agree that even though we mandate a multi-racial slate for SMC contest, we have no control over how the outcome is going to turn out.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, it will not work out according to the quota that we have, but that is where the party list comes in.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Let us say, for example, if we are short of a particular racial group, even though that person may be fifth on the list,  he gets chosen first.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, in that way, you use the party list to make up for any shortfall in racial representation as a result of unpredictable SMC contests.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sorry, just a quick clarification to Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, she thanked the hon Mr Murali for sharing his experience and I also thank Mr Murali for sharing his experience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But she mentioned that it may not matter because he won anyway.
